Investment memo · TEN-IT · NYSE American depositary shares: TS

Tenaris: a quality cyclical whose investment case is front-loaded; own the shares into spring 2027 and exit in the second half of 2027

Written on 4 November 2026, the morning of Tenaris's third-quarter results and the day after the US midterm elections; neither outcome is reflected in this memo. Share price €25.93 (about $29.05 a share). Money is in US dollars unless stated; the conventions are in the end notes.

Ownthe next 6-9 monthsestimate upgrades, a guidance step-up, a confirmed dividend
Exitsecond half of 2027distributor restocking ends; imports and new US mills arrive
Do not pay fora re-ratingthe fair multiple is 12-13x earnings, about where the shares trade

#0. Summary: the investment case on one page

The decisionOwn Tenaris for the next six to nine months, while a US price rise, a guidance step-up and a doubled dividend are confirmed. Sell in the second half of 2027, before earnings fade, because the shares already trade at a fair multiple and offer no re-rating.

What Tenaris is. Tenaris is the world's largest maker of seamless and premium steel pipe for oil and gas wells (oil country tubular goods, or OCTG). It supplies about a third of global OCTG, 40% of premium seamless pipe and 37% of premium connections. It has three times Vallourec's revenue, $3.56bn of net cash, and a service model that no rival has copied: Rig Direct, which carries 70% of group sales and 90% of US sales. Tenaris earns a 20-25% EBITDA margin through the cycle and held a margin floor of about 20% in the downturns of 2016, 2020 and 2024.

What the case is. Tenaris is a quality cyclical entering the most favourable six to nine months of its cycle, on numbers that the sell-side has not yet caught up with. A plateau and a fade follow, which the sell-side's bulls do not foresee. Three developments arrive between now and mid-2027, and each is visible before it reaches the income statement:

  1. 1
    A US price rent reaches Tenaris's income statement. The US seamless OCTG price index rose 9% in October to above $3,100/t, its largest monthly gain since July 2008 and a 26% rise year to date. Tenaris's realised prices follow the index with a lag of one to two quarters, at a stable premium of about 34%. The index is already 9% above the level the base case assumed for end-2026, distributor inventories are below their long-term average at about 4.5 months of supply, and OCTG imports fell 25% month on month in August. The price support is a policy rent (the Section 232 tariff of 50% on full customs value, plus anti-dumping deposits on pipe from Austria, Taiwan and the United Arab Emirates since 30 October) combined with distributor restocking. The rent is real and large, and it has an end date.
  2. 2
    Guidance and consensus are set up to be beaten. Management guides only half a year at a time, excludes any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, gives only qualitative credit to price rises it can already see, and has beaten consensus EPS in 18 of the last 21 quarters. The FactSet median for FY2027 EBITDA ($3,053m) is stale: half the brokers last updated in August, when the index stood at $2,500-2,600/t, and several still divide by 1,027-1,036m shares when 1,009.6m are in issue. The brokers who have updated sit at $3.2-3.6bn, and the model of record has $3,344m.
  3. 3
    The annual dividend has probably doubled, and the dividend consensus has not caught up. Tenaris doubled its 2026 interim dividend to $0.59. Interims have been one-third of the annual total for five years; the CEO chose dividends over buybacks for "simplicity and liquidity"; and Ternium, which has the same controlling shareholder and the same free-float constraint, has made the same choice. A final dividend of about $1.10 in February 2027 implies $1.70-1.80 a year, a 6.2% yield at today's price, against a FactSet dividend consensus of $1.09 for FY2026 and $1.50 for FY2027.

What the case is not. Tenaris is neither a compounder nor a re-rating story. EPS rises from $1.83 in FY2025 to about $2.23 in FY2027, then falls back to about $1.85 by FY2029, as restocking ends, three dated US capacity additions arrive, and operators set their 2028 budgets after the fall in oil prices that a Hormuz reopening would bring. The share count gives no support because buybacks have ended; the 2029 fade carries a 70% decremental margin on price; and the two-year-forward P/E is already 13.0x, the 89th percentile of its five-year range and above its ten-year median of 12.2x. The dashboard's guideline fair multiple of 23.24x (the 90th percentile of ten years) is, in Tenaris's history, a product of trough earnings rather than a premium for peak delivery: the shares traded above 20x only in 2016-18 and 2020-21, when EPS was near zero, and at 6-9x in the peak-earnings years of 2022-23. I do not use the guideline multiple (see #11).

The shape of the return. The model's total return of +60% to December 2027 at the guideline multiple includes 27 points of re-rating that I do not expect. If the multiple holds at 12-13x, the next six to nine months offer roughly +5-10%, from a 7-10% upgrade cycle for FY2027 estimates, two guidance steps and a confirmed 6% yield, with more if the shares re-test April's multiple of 16.5x. After spring 2027, the forward earnings years that the market prices roll from FY2027-28 to FY2028-29, and the earnings contribution to the return turns against the holder. This is an 18-month case, with the exit in the second half of 2027.

The four judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic. The conversions use 1,009.6m shares and a 21% tax rate, so $100m of EBITDA is worth about $0.078 of EPS. Base-case FY2027 EPS after minorities is $2.23.

It also separates a market that trusts the controlling shareholder's capital policy from one that does not.

Grade legend: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. The strengths are current momentum (#8), the guidance record (#4), industry structure (#3) and scope for upgrades (#7). The weaknesses are forecast growth (#6), the fair multiple (#11) and total shareholder return (#12).

#1. Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Key messageThe external environment gives Tenaris a strong tailwind for the next three to four quarters, and that tailwind has an end date. It consists mostly of a US price rent created by trade policy and distributor restocking; the only structural tailwind, deepwater drilling, accounts for about a fifth of revenue.

Evidence. The external environment has swung from a headwind to the strongest short-term tailwind the industry has had since 2022. From 2024 to the first half of 2026, the US seamless index fell to a trough of $2,110/t, the US rig count fell 7%, Saudi Aramco ran down its pipe inventories, a 50% tariff hit Tenaris's imported steel billets, and the Strait of Hormuz has been closed since March 2026. The evidence of the swing:

  • US pipe prices: seamless up 26% year to date and welded up 33%.
  • US drilling: the rig count is up about 10% this year to about 600, with private and independent operators adding about 50 rigs. Pipe used per rig rises 3-4% a year as horizontal laterals lengthen, so pipe makers gain from the same drilling efficiency that hurts service companies paid per rig.
  • US supply and trade: distributor inventories are trending down to about 4.5 months of supply against a 5.5-month median; OCTG imports fell 25% month on month in August to 113kt; preliminary anti-dumping determinations against Austria, Taiwan and the United Arab Emirates on 30 October allege dumping margins of 44-126%; and a US Department of Justice trade-fraud task force is prosecuting transhipment.
  • Offshore, the only demand segment with two or more years of visibility: spending steps up about 30% in 2027 (Saipem research: $149bn from $115bn, 71% of it greenfield). Petrobras has a $78bn plan, ExxonMobil has awarded Tenaris a ten-year Stabroek contract, TotalEnergies is standardising all 36 Suriname wells on Tenaris connections, and ADNOC has extended its $1.9bn contract.
  • Oil price: Brent at $105-111 a barrel funds operators' budgets.

Inference. The three tailwinds differ in quality. The deepwater cycle is structural and visible to 2028, but it is only about 20% of revenue. The US price rent is the largest tailwind and reaches the income statement over the next two to four quarters, but it is built from policy (Section 232 plus anti-dumping duties) and from distributor restocking, and both will end. Restocking ends once distributors hold five to six months of supply; the policy support ends whenever Washington bargains it away. Rising drilling intensity is a small, steady and mechanical positive.

Three headwinds stand against these tailwinds. First, input costs: hot-rolled coil costs $1,375-1,385/t, up $380/t since January; scrap is up 20-30%; and Tenaris's coil contract with Nucor's Hickman mill expires in December. These costs squeeze welded-pipe margins by $35-40m a quarter and reach cost of goods sold with a two-quarter lag. Second, the Hormuz closure defers 30-40kt and $120-130m of premium Gulf revenue a quarter, and has lifted selling, general and administrative costs by about $30m a quarter. Third, onshore South America outside Argentina is weak: Colombia's rig count fell from 50 to 28, the Ecuador mill is idle, and Tenaris lost the Argentine pipeline tender to Welspun, which bid 31% lower.

So what. Two external variables, both published monthly, are the investment case. Of the FY2027 EBITDA step-up of about $565m, 64% comes from US price, 20% from the return of Gulf revenue and 18% from other volume; tariff mitigation and the Artrom acquisition roughly offset fixed-cost inflation and the lagged rise in input costs.

Strongest counter-case. By this industry's own record, the October price jump is a late-cycle signal. The last monthly gain of this size, in 2008, preceded a halving of the US rig count within months; in 2018, the tariff-driven price surge flattened within five months, once distributors had built 8.5 months of stock. Seamless imports also rose 48% month on month in August even as welded imports fell, which shows that importers already find it profitable to pay the tariff: US coil at $1,380/t compares with a tariff-inclusive import parity of $900-920/t.

What would change my view. Upwards: a Hormuz reopening before February with Brent holding above $85, or the US rig count rising towards 620. Downwards: two consecutive monthly falls in the PipeLogix seamless index; imports up more than 20-25% over three months; distributor inventories above six months of supply; or any Section 232 exemption or trade deal after the midterm elections.

Against the market. The sell-side knows every fact above and treats the price rise as a tariff effect, but no broker dates its end: Redburn holds a realised price of $3,283/t through 2028, and Morgan Stanley holds $3,410/t. I date the end of the price rent to the second half of 2027. I also link a Hormuz reopening to a lower oil price (Deutsche Bank expects $74 a barrel on a settlement), which reaches the US rig count through the 2028 budget round; no Tenaris analyst makes that connection.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. The external swing is large and near-term: US seamless pricing is up 26% this year, distributor stocks are lean, imports are falling, and deepwater spending steps up 30% in 2027, together adding about 10% to FY2027 revenue and most of a $565m EBITDA step. But the biggest component is a policy-and-restocking price rent that Section 232 bargaining or a completed restocking can end. The only structural component, deepwater, is about a fifth of sales, and input costs, the Hormuz deferral and weak South American onshore demand offset part of the gain, so over two to three years the net positive fades to flat revenue in 2028 and a fall in 2029. I agree with the group's 64 and place Tenaris a little above Linea Directa's advanced, reversible cycle, but below Eckert & Ziegler's structural demand.

#2. Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Key messageInternal change is neutral for EPS and positive for cash returns. The February 2027 dividend decision is the one internal event that can move the shares.

Evidence.

  • Leadership: Gabriel Podskubka became CEO on 6 May 2026, the first CEO from outside the Rocca family, after 31 years in the group and three as chief operating officer running the tariff response. Paolo Rocca remains Chairman.
  • Tariff response, which was fast: Bay City runs at record output; Koppel's heat-treatment and finishing lines restarted in January; a framework agreement secures steel bars from Nucor's Memphis mill; a $90m upgrade of Koppel and Ambridge runs into the second half of 2027; and the CAD 306m modernisation of Sault Ste. Marie carries CAD 148m of public money. The quarterly tariff cost fell from about $150m to $110-120m by May 2026.
  • Rig Direct's extension: offshore (a 74,500m² Suriname base for TotalEnergies and a Guyana base for ExxonMobil's 35-well campaign) and digital (the WISer and AllTorque services, and a Houston centre monitoring 70 rigs).
  • Artrom, Romania: an €86m acquisition of 200kt of seamless capacity and 450kt of steelmaking capacity inside the EU's import-quota wall, closing this quarter.
  • Costs: headcount fell by 3,260 in 2024 and by about 1,000 in 2025, and half of a $200m cost programme was delivered within four quarters.
  • Capital returns, the one real change: Tenaris terminated its second buyback tranche in March after $584m of $600m, doubled the interim dividend, and authorised no new buyback.

Inference. Tenaris is not a corporate-change story. The leadership succession is orderly and preserves the Rocca industrial culture of engineering, margin over volume and counter-cyclical investment. Regionalised production is the right answer to today's trade policy, but it raises the North American fixed-cost base by perhaps $50-100m a year plus $20-30m of depreciation. That extra fixed cost helps while the US market is busy and protected, and hurts if the US rig count falls below about 540-550.

The capital-return pivot is the internal force that matters. I read it as a larger ordinary dividend replacing the buyback at roughly the old combined total of $2.2bn, not as a halving of distributions. The free-float constraint (San Faustin, the controlling shareholder, owns 66% of the capital and 70% of the votes, and Milan requires a 25% minimum free float) limits the pace of buybacks rather than ruling them out. The choice of dividends therefore reflects the controlling shareholder's preference for cash, which it needs for Tecpetrol's $6.4bn Vaca Muerta programme and Ternium's capital spending at Pesquería, and the family's liking for simplicity.

So what. Internal forces add little to EPS: there is no new cost programme and no buyback, fixed costs are edging up, and management calls Artrom "non-material". The end of buybacks also removes the 4-7% a year of EPS support that share-count reduction gave in 2024-25. Internal forces add a lot to total return if the dividend is confirmed at about $1.80.

Strongest counter-case. The dividend pivot could be the first sign of a controlling shareholder putting group liquidity ahead of minority shareholders. Ternium cut its own proposed 2025 dividend from $2.70 to $2.20 per American depositary share in April 2026 when cash got tight, which shows that a board controlled by the Techint group will trim payouts when it wants cash. Two further governance warnings: working capital stands at 143 days (against 128 a year earlier and Vallourec's 86), and the CEO's pay is all cash with no financial targets.

What would change my view. A final dividend of $0.60-0.75 in February, which I put at 40%, would mean that total distributions really have halved and that cash is being hoarded. A buyback authorisation used in 2027, which I put at 35-45%, would be an upside surprise.

Against the market. Jefferies and Redburn read the interim dividend as one-third of an annual total of about $1.80. The FactSet dividend consensus ($1.09 for FY2026 and $1.50 for FY2027) and Morgan Stanley's model, which still assumes a $1.2bn buyback in July, do not. I side with the two brokers that have done the arithmetic; the February announcement settles the question.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. Internal change is a matter of form rather than strategy. The orderly CEO succession, the fast tariff response (the Koppel restart, US bar sourcing, the quarterly tariff cost cut from $150m to $110-120m), Rig Direct's move offshore and Artrom are sensible but small for earnings. Against them, the buyback that gave 4-7% a year of EPS support has ended, regionalisation adds $50-100m a year of fixed cost, working capital has slipped to 143 days, and the doubled dividend is a cash-return choice rather than an earnings force. Net, internal change is a mild negative for EPS within three years, just below Reply's change-free continuity and above Indus's externally driven raise, and in line with the group's 46.

#3. Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Key messageA wide moat, built mostly on mills and customer qualification, and a fortress balance sheet protect the 20% margin floor and justify a valuation premium to tubular peers. Margin parity with Vallourec and a weak US steel supply chain cap how far that premium can grow.

Evidence.

  • Industry structure: premium seamless pipe is a tight oligopoly in which the top three (Tenaris 40%, Vallourec 26%, Nippon Steel 18%) hold 84%. Entry requires a hot-rolling mill plus two to three years of qualification with national oil companies. Global seamless capacity has been flat at 21.2mt since 2018 and is about 3% short of demand, the first deficit since 2013, after US Steel idled 1.1mt and Vallourec closed 1.15mt.
  • Competitor behaviour: rational. Vallourec caps shipments at 1.7mt, returns 80-100% of its cash and has no equivalent of Rig Direct. Of OCTG volume, 40-45% is now on multi-year contracts at a 5-10% premium to spot.
  • Tenaris's price premium: realised prices sit 34% above the index because Rig Direct replaces the customer's own procurement function (531 rigs, 44 warehouses), an organisational switching cost.
  • Financial profile: a decade-average Tubes EBITDA margin of 21%, against Vallourec's 4% before its restructuring; post-tax return on invested capital of about 15% at FY2025 margins and 28% at the 2023 peak; cash conversion before dividends of 99-113% of net income in FY2023-25; net cash of $3.56bn on the company's basis, with $450m of debt; and capex of about $600m, roughly equal to depreciation.
  • Management: Paolo Rocca grew revenue from $2.8bn to $12bn, bought Hydril (2007) and IPSCO (2020, in the trough), walked away from Benteler on antitrust grounds, and cut fixed costs 25% in 2020. The senior bench averages 25 years in the group, and resignations of professional staff are at a ten-year low of 3.6%.

Inference. The industry structure underwrites the 20% margin floor, Tenaris's share of premium pipe and its contract renewals. It no longer underwrites a margin lead. Vallourec has earned a margin at or above 20% for 13 quarters, made $724/t of Tubes EBITDA in the first quarter of 2026, and matched Tenaris's margin in the second quarter (21.4% against 21.9%). Vallourec is also 100% self-sufficient in US steel at Youngstown, whereas Tenaris buys about 1.14mt of steel externally and imports about 28% of its North American billets under the tariff. The supply side, not demand, is Tenaris's structural weak link.

For management, the test is shareholder alignment rather than operating skill. Only four of ten directors are independent, there is no nomination or remuneration committee, insiders own 0.08% of the shares, and executive incentives rest on safety and decarbonisation rather than financial targets. Minority shareholders are aligned with the controlling shareholder through ownership (San Faustin receives 66% of every dollar paid out), not through governance.

So what. Tenaris deserves a valuation premium to its tubular peers for its balance sheet, its service lock-in and its dividend capacity: it trades at 13.0x P/E and about 8.4x EV/EBITDA, against Vallourec's 8.1x and 5.2x. Its economics relative to peers have stopped improving, however, so the premium should be held, not extrapolated.

Tubes are about 95% of revenue, and consensus already has Tubes revenue flat from FY2027 to FY2028, the plateau that this memo expects.

Strongest counter-case. Scale no longer gives lower unit costs in pipe milling. National champions (Saudi Arabia's JESCO and AMTJ, and Vallourec in Brazil) are taking share under local-content rules. Chinese mills have copied premium connections and hold 90% of their home market. And the combination of Nippon Steel and US Steel is a well-funded adjacent entrant, with an $11bn US investment programme to 2028, a $475m quench-and-temper line at Fairfield for 2029 and a $75m premium-thread line sooner.

What would change my view. Evidence that Vallourec's margin is moving ahead of Tenaris's rather than level with it, or the loss of a Rig Direct customer, would cut the quality premium. A counter-cyclical acquisition at the next trough would confirm it.

Against the market. The market already values Tenaris alongside the offshore-scarcity group (Saipem at 12.6x, Subsea 7 at 12.3x, Gaztransport & Technigaz at 15.4x) rather than alongside tubular makers. I agree that the balance sheet and service model justify that choice of peer group; I disagree that the valuation gap to Vallourec can widen further from here.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. The qualitative inputs are strong. Tenaris is number one in a three-player premium seamless oligopoly holding 84%, protected by mill-plus-qualification barriers and the Rig Direct procurement lock-in, with $3.56bn of net cash, capex near depreciation and a 20% EBITDA floor held through downturns. It is held back by cyclicality (EPS ranged from -$0.54 to $3.32 in six years, so predictability is low), by a margin lead over Vallourec that has gone, by a tariffed external steel supply and by governance that puts the controlling shareholder first. A return on invested capital of 11.3% (71st percentile), and about 15% mid-cycle on capital that now earns only about the old margin, confirms a sound rather than elite profile. That places Tenaris with Volex-like quality, just under Theon, coherent with the groups' 64-74.

#4. Conservative guidance, conservative expectations, and the delivery record

Key messageTenaris's guidance is conservative by construction. The next two events are 70-80% likely to meet expectations and step guidance up; from August 2027, the same guidance culture turns the half-yearly steps against the stock.

Evidence. Guidance for the second half of 2026 is "in line with the first half" ($6.07bn of sales and $1.38bn of EBITDA). It explicitly assumes that Hormuz stays closed through the year end, with the third quarter seasonally lower and fourth-quarter shipments above 1mt "on higher pricing". Annualised, that guidance sits about 1-2% above the FactSet median for FY2026 ($11.89bn of sales and $2.73bn of EBITDA) and in line with the named brokers ($12.06-12.41bn of sales).

  • The beat record: EPS beats in 18 of 21 quarters. The fourth-quarter 2025 margin was 23.9% against 22.6% expected; first-quarter 2026 EBITDA was $735m against $707m; second-quarter 2026 net income beat by 10%, though through a lower-quality financial-income beat, with EBITDA in line.
  • Margin resilience: margins stayed inside a 20-25% corridor through a 17% revenue fall in 2023-24, when sector margins typically compress by 400-600 basis points. Over a decade, bearish downgrades of this stock were right only about a third of the time.
  • Guidance habit: Tenaris never raises guidance formally. It reiterates, beats, and lets the next half-year outlook step up. Informal commentary runs ahead of the formal numbers: management speaks of offshore "impeccable execution opportunities" through 2028 and of "upside in activity, sales and prices".

Quarterly margins stayed inside the 20-25% corridor through the 2024-26 down-leg, with the second quarter of 2026 the trough.

Inference. The beat habit is mechanical and repeatable for the next two events. Realised prices lag a public index by one to two quarters, so management already sees the next two quarters' prices when it guides, and it guides below them. The beat habit says nothing about the cycle, however: the 2024 beats came while consensus was being cut.

My probabilities for the next events are set out in the timeline below. The odds favour the holder at the third-quarter results and in February 2027. From the August 2027 outlook onwards they even out, and the February 2028 guidance for the first half of 2028 is more likely to sit below the second half of 2027 than above it.

So what. The favourable gap between what the company will say and what the market expects is concentrated in the next two events. After that, the same guidance culture trims expectations promptly, as it did in August 2026.

Strongest counter-case. The risk to the near-term upside is cost, not demand. Tenaris's 140 days of inventory carry today's coil and scrap prices into the first half of 2027, the Nucor coil contract is renewed in December, and the squeeze on welded-pipe margins is $35-40m a quarter. A February outlook "in line with" rather than "above" the second half of 2026 is the 20% case, and the bulls would read it as a miss.

What would change my view. Third-quarter EBITDA below $630m, or fourth-quarter commentary that does not strengthen on price, would show that the lag between the index and realised prices is longer than one to two quarters.

Against the market. The market expects beats, and Jefferies calls the guidance "deliberately conservative". The difference between my view and the market's is the size of the beat: the consensus median has not priced the October index at all, and I think the February outlook is more likely to show a visible step up than the market's assumption of another "in line" outlook allows.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Tenaris has beaten consensus EPS in 18 of 21 quarters and kept margins inside the 20-25% corridor through a 17% revenue fall. Its current half-year guidance is conservative by construction, because realised prices lag a public index that management already sees. It sits below Maersk because it never formally raises guidance, it trimmed promptly in August 2026, and its 2024-25 beats came while consensus was being cut, but above Odfjell's beats, which were assisted by one-off items. I rate it above the groups' 62-64 because the repeatable beat mechanism and the current conservatism are well evidenced.

#5. Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Key messageTenaris's profits are geared to price, not volume. A 4x price lever with 55-65% first-year drop-through turns a 10% revenue rise into a 20% EBITDA rise in 2027; the same lever, at a 70% decremental margin, drives the 2029 fade.

Evidence. Operating leverage is asymmetric: it depends on whether price or volume moves, and in which direction.

Driver of revenue changeEBITDA per dollar of revenue changeEvidence
Volume upAbout 45 cents (volume leverage 1.7-2.0x)Incremental margins of 43% in FY2022 and 41% in FY2023; fixed cash costs of $2.0-3.0bn (Bernstein's 2024 fixed base was $2,649m, including $632m of depreciation)
Price upAbout 4x leverage before input costs (revenue over EBITDA), damped to 55-65 cents in the first yearScrap and billet costs follow pipe prices with an 80% correlation and a lag of up to 12 months
Volume down36-40 cents, cushioned by cost cutsIn 2020 Tenaris cut fixed costs 25% ($230m a year) within three quarters
Price downAbout 70 centsIn 2024 revenue fell $2.3bn and EBITDA fell $1.7bn
  • Fixed costs ratchet up in upturns: they rose 55% from 2021 to 2024 on 92% revenue growth, with more than 4,000 shop-floor hires. Two-thirds of the workforce is unionised, with wage indexation in Argentina and Brazil.
  • No financial leverage: net cash earns about $125-155m a year, and a 100-basis-point change in US dollar interest rates moves EPS by about $0.03.
  • Cost scope in this upturn is specific and external: tariff mitigation adds $80m in 2027 and $150m in 2028, capped at about a third of the gross tariff cost because domestic bars carry protected prices; the end of Hormuz freight costs adds $60m in 2027 and $120m a year from 2028. Against these, fixed-cost inflation runs at $60-80m a year.

Inference. Revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth only when the growth comes from price. In 2027, revenue growth of 10% becomes EBITDA growth of 20% and EPS growth of 14%, after a higher tax rate and flat non-operating income. The same mechanism runs in reverse at a 70% decremental margin on the way down, which is why the base case's 4% revenue fall in FY2029 becomes a 12% fall in EBITDA and a 14% fall in EPS.

The reinforcing feedback loops dominate until about the end of 2027: the tariff, falling imports, rising prices and restocking; the Rig Direct lock-in; and the global seamless deficit. The balancing loops take over during 2028: restocking ends by construction; Welspun's 350kt high-frequency-induction-welded mill is complete and its 300kt longitudinal-submerged-arc-welded mill is due; Borusan adds 950kt; U.S. Steel builds at Fairfield; Tenaris's own Koppel capacity returns; and fixed costs ratchet up. The link between Hormuz and the oil price is a self-hedge that narrows the range of outcomes in both directions: a reopening restores Gulf revenue but lowers the oil price behind US drilling budgets.

So what. The investor is paid for price, not volume, and price is the variable that Tenaris does not control. Operating leverage works strongly in the holder's favour for the next four quarters and dangerously against the holder from 2028. The net-cash balance sheet removes any financing risk from that down-leg.

Strongest counter-case. Tenaris's own pricing power is demonstrable: a stable 34% premium to the index, variable margins that rose 15-20% through 20-30% input-cost inflation, and formula pass-through in contracts with national oil companies. The price rent might also last. The final anti-dumping rulings in January-March 2027, findings under the Enforce and Protect Act and Department of Justice enforcement are structural barriers that were absent in 2008 and 2018, so the price plateau could be higher and longer than in any previous cycle (Redburn's argument that prices will settle "12% above the long-term average").

What would change my view. Welded imports resuming at the July 2026 pace (+81% month on month), or a Nucor coil renewal at spot prices, would show that costs will eat the price rent sooner. A second year of a flat-to-rising index with imports contained would show that the policy floor is structural.

Against the market. Bernstein frames Tenaris's leverage as upside ("operating leverage ahead?"); no broker frames the 70% decremental margin and the fixed-cost ratchet on the way down. Consensus for FY2028 already has flat Tubes revenue, so the median agrees with my plateau; the bulls do not.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Operating leverage is real and proven in both directions: an incremental margin of about 45% on volume, a 4x price lever with 55-65% first-year drop-through (FY2027 revenue growth of 10% gives EBITDA growth of 20%), and a 25% fixed-cost cut delivered within three quarters in 2020. The company also holds a stable 34% price premium over the index. It falls short of the 75 level because the price it gears into is an industry rent it does not control, fixed costs ratchet up in upturns, there is no financial leverage (Tenaris has net cash), and the reinforcing loops give way to balancing ones from 2028. Even in the up year, EPS grows only about 1.4 times as fast as revenue.

Inference. EPS grows about 6% a year from FY2025 to FY2028 (consensus: 5%), entirely from operating profit, and then dips. Compared with the last six years (revenue of $5.1-14.9bn, margins of 12-32% and EPS of -$0.54 to $3.32), the next four years sit in a narrow band: revenue of $12.2-13.5bn, margins of 22-25% and EPS of $1.85-2.25. Only FY2027 shows double-digit growth, with EPS up 14%.

Margins do not exceed their past peaks: the 2027 peak of 24.9% compares with 32.4% in 2023, because this cycle's price rent (tariffs plus restocking) is smaller and more fragile than 2022's (a demand shock plus the exit of Russian supply). Free cash flow is lower than in FY2023-25 but steadier. With a $1.80 dividend costing $1.82bn, about 90-95% of free cash flow after leases, net cash stays near $3.6-4.0bn on the company's basis rather than climbing to $5bn.

Over the last seven years the EBITDA margin swung between 12% and 32%; the forecasts above stay inside 22-25%.

So what. Double-digit growth is a one-year event, and there is no scope for growth or margins above past levels over four years. The forecasts are mildly positive for an 18-month case (FY2026-27 above consensus, strong cash flow and a confirmed yield) and neutral to negative beyond it (no compounding, a cyclical fade, and a dividend that absorbs most free cash flow).

Strongest counter-case. The bull cases are coherent, not reckless. Redburn's 25.6% margin and $2.70 of 2028 EPS need only the index to hold at today's level and the tariffs to stay. Morgan Stanley's $2.50 for FY2027 is 12% above my base case. A probability-weighted FY2027 (bull 30%, base 50%, bear 15%, severe 5%) gives EBITDA of $3.27bn and EPS of $2.17, within 1% of the consensus mean, so the expected value is close to where the better-informed brokers already sit.

What would change my view. A fourth-quarter 2026 margin above 24% and a first-half 2027 outlook above the second half of 2026 would move me towards the bull path for 2027. Distributor inventories above six months of supply, or seamless imports above about 60kt a month, would bring the 2028 fade forward.

Against the market. My forecasts are above the consensus median for FY2026-27 (EBITDA higher by 2% and 9.5%; EPS by 4% and 8% like for like), on the median for FY2028, and below the two-broker figure for FY2029. Several brokers' outdated share counts depress consensus EPS by 2-3%, so the true gap between my FY2027 EPS and consensus is about 6%, not 11%.

The FactSet median has FY2027 EBITDA at $3,053m and the FY2027 dividend at $1.50, both below this memo's figures.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. Growth of nil to 5% gives a D, and I place Tenaris at the floor of that band. The path is a one-year EPS rise of 14% in FY2027 followed by a plateau and a dip, with margins peaking at 24.9% against 32% in 2023, and with no help from buybacks. Consensus EPS growth over two to three years of -10% (4th percentile) confirms that the measure is not understating the fade.

#7. Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over 6-12 months

Key messageFY2027 consensus is set to rise 7-10% over the next two events, with most brokers raising, and the dividend consensus is set to be reset higher. After that, the upgrade cycle has nowhere further to go.

Evidence. The FY2027 median EBITDA of $3,053m mixes stale and current estimates, as the chart below shows. The low half (Oddo at $2,865m, Zephirin at $2,915m, and five Italian and North American brokers at $3,016-3,118m) mostly last updated in August, before the September and October index prints (+16% and +26% year to date) and before the inventory data. The brokers that updated later (Jefferies on 29 September, Goldman Sachs, a restricted broker on 12 October, Morgan Stanley and Redburn) sit at $3,207-3,630m.

  • FY2027 EPS: median $2.06 and mean $2.12, or about $2.10 and $2.16 on the true share count.
  • Coverage: twelve brokers forecast FY2027, ten forecast FY2028 and two forecast FY2029.
  • Ratings: 14% Buy, a Hold on average, and price targets of $25-39 a share against a price of $29.05; the mean target of $32.64 is 12% above the price.

Inference. FY2027 consensus EBITDA and EPS are more likely to rise 7-10% than to fall over the next two events, and the upgrades should be broad: six to eight of the twelve brokers raising in November, and more in February, when a first-half 2027 outlook above the second half of 2026 forces models built "flat on the second half" to move. Four mechanisms stack up:

  1. The price lag: an index 9% above the model inputs, applied to the 30-43% of sales linked to it, is worth $150-250m of 2027 EBITDA before cost offsets.
  2. The guidance step in February.
  3. The share-count correction: brokers moving to the true share count adds 2-3% to EPS with no change in profit.
  4. Vallourec's own US drop-through ($150-200/t), which the same analysts are upgrading.

The dividend is the single consensus number most likely to be revised sharply, from $1.09 and $1.50 towards $1.19 and $1.70-1.80. Ratings follow estimates: the 14% Buy share is held down by valuation, not by earnings, so I expect it to rise towards 30-40% into the first quarter of 2027 as price targets follow the numbers. The narrative moves from "tariff winner" to "tariff winner with a 6% yield and FY2027 EBITDA above $3.3bn".

The broker sheets show the August-dated brokers at the bottom of the FY2027 range and the late-September and October updates at the top.

So what. The favourable gap between my assessment and the market's is real, dated and front-loaded. It is worth about 7-10% on FY2027 numbers and about two points of dividend yield, and it is delivered at two events (4 November and 18 February) plus the annual general meeting in May.

Strongest counter-case. The expected-value gap is small because the tails are fat. Excluding the stale brokers, the updated brokers already carry $3.2-3.6bn, so a FY2027 upgrade is partly a median catching up with the mean, which the share price may already discount after a 74% rise in twelve months. Brokers focused on costs (one research note is titled "Caveat COGS") will hold margin forecasts down, and the two brokers with thin estimates ($1.69-1.81 of EPS) may not update at all.

What would change my view. A February outlook "in line with" the second half of 2026 (20% probability), a final dividend of $0.60-0.75 (40%), or a tariff exemption after the midterms would stop the upgrade cycle before it reaches the median.

Against the market. The market knows the direction of revisions but not their size. The market's narrative does not make four connections: the price rise to its end date; the Hormuz reopening to the oil price and the 2028 budget round; the doubled interim dividend to a doubled annual dividend; and the outdated share count to the EPS median. Those four connections are my edge for six months and my warning for eighteen.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is about 70% likely to step up in practice in February, with the outlook for the first half of 2027 above the second half of 2026 as realised prices catch up with the October index. The FY2027 consensus median looks set to rise 7-10% as the August-dated brokers update and the share count is corrected, about one times the 4-10% revenue growth rate (near the 76th percentile), and the dividend consensus is likely to reset from $1.50 towards $1.70-1.80. The narrative improves only modestly. Part of the upgrade is a median catching up with an already higher mean and with updated brokers at $3.2-3.6bn, and the window closes after the next two events, so Tenaris sits just below AT&S and above Munters, slightly above the group's 66.

Key messageSell-side and technical momentum are both graded B, and estimate momentum is about to accelerate. The fragilities are a risk-off market, the stock's 40% exposure to energy-services sector moves, and its outlier run against tubular peers.

Inference. Momentum differs by measure. Estimate momentum is positive and about to re-accelerate, because the October data arrived after most of the series was compiled. Price momentum is positive but tired: the shares have paused for six months after a nine-month run. (The three-month rise in price targets is more informative than the one-month fall of 11%, which looks like a currency or basis artefact.) Guidance momentum is neutral until February. Tenaris is the outlier among tubular makers and a member in good standing of the offshore group. About 60% of its share-price movement is specific to the company and about 40% follows energy-services stocks, with a beta of about 1.1 to that basket.

So what. The market rewards Tenaris's own delivery (the 60% of share-price movement specific to the company), so the November and February results can move the stock. But the 40% that follows the sector is tied to oil through the offshore names, and the most likely fundamental positive for Tenaris, a Hormuz reopening, is a negative for that group's valuation multiples. In that event, expect Tenaris's shares to lag its own earnings.

Strongest counter-case. Two rules from Viewforth's Wisdom Library apply to a stock up 74% while its tubular peers are up 5-15%: an extended trend means the upside is already banked, and an outlier's relative strength tends to fade back towards its peer group's. A risk-off market sells high-momentum cyclicals first. And the sell-side's average Hold rating, unusual for a stock up 74%, means there are no committed bulls to defend the shares on a miss.

What would change my view. A break below the 200-day average (about €23.9) with falling estimates would end the momentum case; a beat on US drop-through in Vallourec's third-quarter results would confirm it.

Against the market. I agree with the dashboard's grades of B for sell-side momentum, B for technicals and C for valuation. Where I differ is on the peer group: the Wisdom Library's "outlier" warning is right if Tenaris's peers are the tubular makers and wrong if they are energy-services companies, and the market has chosen energy services.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures are in the top fifth and no part is clearly negative: the price is 8% above a rising 200-day average, FY2027 EPS is up 9% over six months (82nd percentile), price targets are up 19% over six months, and the Buy share is up 8 points. Weak tubular peers do not pull the grade down on their own. I place it at the floor of A because guidance has only been reiterated, the three-month revision is just +1% (55th percentile), the price has paused for six months and the market regime is risk-off.

#9. Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Key messageThe case is simple and trackable, with a well-cushioned fundamental floor. The real risk is that the share price (a top-decile multiple, 40% exposure to energy-services moves, an outlier run) is more exposed than earnings, and past cycles put the price peak 6-12 months away.

Simplicity. The case turns on one price variable, one timing variable and one policy variable. Two external drivers, the US seamless index and the timing of the Hormuz reopening, generate about 85% of the FY2027 EBITDA step-up and about 80% of the 2028-29 reversal. Both are published monthly or daily and lead the income statement by one to two quarters. That is concentration of the useful kind: the case is exposed to few things, and each of them can be tracked.

Sector and cyclical precedents. Every record monthly rise in US OCTG prices has been followed by a correction within 6-12 months, as the table below shows. In past cycles, distributor months of supply was the earliest signal. What differs this time is tighter inventories (4.5 months, against 7-8.5 months at previous peaks) and a policy floor (tariffs on full customs value, anti-dumping deposits and Department of Justice enforcement against transhipment). Both argue for a higher and longer price plateau, not for the absence of a correction.

Fair trough. The fair trough share price is about €15-17, 35-45% below today: EBITDA of $2.0bn at 6x, plus about $4.8bn of net non-operating assets. A de-rating alone, to the five-year median P/E of 9.46x on $2.09 of EPS, gives about €17.6 (-32%). The published bear cases cluster at €13-16 (Redburn €15; Jefferies €16; Morgan Stanley $30 per American depositary share, about €13.4). Net cash, about 12-15% of the equity value, cushions the fall relative to peers.

Strongest counter-case against calling the shares risky. Very low short interest, options used only for hedging, a Hold-heavy sell-side, no financial leverage, low customer concentration (the largest customer is about 10% of sales), formula pricing on 55-70% of revenue, and the self-hedge between Hormuz and the oil price all argue that realised volatility will be lower than the risk table suggests.

What would change my view. The seven indicators in the table below, plus the February final dividend, form the monitoring set.

Against the market. The brokers have quantified the bear case (a tariff reversal plus oil below $65), so it is less likely to surprise than an unmodelled risk would be. What they have not quantified is the ordinary cyclical fade from a record-month price peak, which is my base case rather than a tail risk.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. The case is simple and trackable, with two monthly published drivers setting about 85% of the FY2027 step-up, and net cash removes any balance-sheet tail. But the memo's FY2027 EPS range of $1.70-2.45 around $2.23 (-24% to +10%) is skewed down. A Section 232 exemption is a sudden, overnight policy binary, and every previous record OCTG price rise was corrected within 6-12 months, with a fair trough 35-45% below the price. That is close to OMV Petrom, where net cash flatters policy and commodity risk, and a little above Fevertree, coherent with the groups' 42 and 52.

#10. Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Key messageTenaris is mid-to-late in its Reinforcing phase. The earnings leg is still to come and the multiple leg is already banked; the thesis broadens into the February results and stalls in the second half of 2027.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule puts the starting phase at Reinforcing, on a two-year-forward P/E of 13.0x, technical momentum of B and sell-side momentum of B. The share price has completed its re-rating leg: the multiple rose from 8x in 2024 to 16.5x in April 2026 and stands at 13x now, with the price up 74% in twelve months. The shares have paused for six months while the market absorbed the Hormuz drag and the end of buybacks. The fundamental and narrative sequences ahead are set out below.

Inference. The thesis broadens over the next two events, as earnings beat a stale consensus and the dividend is confirmed. It stalls during the second half of 2027, when the August outlook is likely to be "in line", imports and new mills become visible, the Gulf catch-up has already landed, and operators set their 2028 budgets at a lower oil price. In OCTG, pipe makers' shares have peaked when distributors rebuild stock and imports return, often while reported earnings are still rising, and that point is more likely to come in the second half of 2027 than before it.

So what. The right posture is to own the reinforcing leg (the next two sets of results and the dividend) and to treat the second half of 2027 as the window to exit, not to add. The lifecycle view, rather than the earnings view, sets the fair multiple in #11.

Strongest counter-case. A policy floor, tight inventories and a deepwater cycle that peaks in 2028 could together extend the Reinforcing phase through 2028. In that case the thesis would keep broadening for 18 months rather than nine, and the bulls' $2.50-2.70 of 2028 EPS would become the forward year that the market prices.

What would change my view. Distributor inventories still below five months of supply, with imports still falling, in the second quarter of 2027 would push the stall out by two to three quarters. A tariff exemption would move the stock straight from Reinforcing to collapsing, without a stall.

Against the market. The sell-side narrative is in the "thesis broadening" stage, and the bulls extrapolate it. I agree with them about the next nine months and disagree about 2028.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's mid-to-late Reinforcing phase. The earnings leg still has six to nine months of broadening (a stale consensus, a February outlook step and dividend confirmation), but the re-rating from 8x to 13x is banked. On this industry's precedents, the stock peaks when distributors refill and imports return, which is likely in the second half of 2027 while earnings are still rising. That is better than BP's late Reinforcing phase at a commodity peak, but behind Nexans' paused Reinforcing phase with growth ahead.

#11. The fair multiple

Key messageThe guideline multiple of 23.24x is a percentile drawn from trough-earnings years and misapplied to a peak-earnings phase. The fair multiple is 12-13x, about where the shares already trade, so the return has to come from earnings and dividends rather than re-rating.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline for a stock in the Reinforcing phase is the 90th percentile of its own ten-year range of two-year-forward P/E: for Tenaris, 23.24x, 79% above today's 13.0x. The ten-year percentiles are 6.4x (10th), 10.1x (35th), 12.2x (median), 17.1x (75th) and 23.2x (90th). The five-year range is 5.98-16.03x, with a median of 9.46x, and today's multiple sits at the 89th percentile of five years.

My view. The guideline does not fit this stock, and the reason lies in Tenaris's own valuation history. Its high multiples are products of trough earnings: 20-35x from late 2016 to early 2018, when EPS was near zero and the price was €8-12, and 18-34x from April 2020 to March 2021, in the Covid trough, at a price of €3-8. Its peak-earnings years traded at the bottom of the range: 6-9x through 2022-23, at €10-14, while EPS was $2.2-3.3. The 2024-25 upturn re-rated the shares from 8x to 10-11x, and the 2026 tariff-and-offshore narrative took them to 16.5x in April and 13x now.

For a cyclical whose earnings are about to peak, history supports a multiple at the low end of the range. The multiple Tenaris already trades on (13x) is above the ten-year median and well above any multiple it carried when EPS was at today's level. The energy-services peers it trades with sit at 8-15x, and Vallourec, with the same margin and no net cash, trades at 8.1x.

My fair multiple is 12-13x two-year-forward earnings. The anchor is the ten-year median of 12.2x (the "prudent" band); up to 13x is justified while the forward years are FY2027-28 and the dividend is being confirmed; and the multiple should move towards 11-12x once the forward years roll to FY2028-29 and the fade comes into view. That means holding the multiple for the next six to nine months and expecting a de-rating over the twelve months after. The premium to tubular peers (for net cash, Rig Direct, the dividend and share liquidity) is earned, and I keep it. A premium to the offshore group is not earned, because Tenaris's visible earnings peak comes before theirs.

What would change my view. Evidence that the policy floor makes 2028 a second year of 25% margins (the Redburn case) would justify holding 13-14x through 2027, and a restart of buybacks would add about one point to the multiple. A tariff reversal would take the multiple back to its 2024 level of 8-9x, on falling earnings.

Against the market. The market's 13x is close to my fair multiple, and I read the dashboard's valuation grade of C as "fair, not cheap". I differ from the guideline, not from the share price.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Neutral on one measure and dear on the other gives a D. The neutral reading flatters, because the ten-year range is lifted by trough-earnings multiples of 20-35x, while peak-earnings years traded at 6-9x and 13x sits at the 89th percentile of five years. Part of the premium to the offshore group is deserved (net cash, Rig Direct, the dividend), and the memo's own fair multiple of 12-13x is about today's multiple, so I place it in the lower middle of the band.

#12. Total shareholder return, Dupont split

Key messageThe model's +60% return includes 27 points of re-rating that I do not expect. At a held multiple, the case returns +5-10% over six to nine months and roughly nothing over 18 months to three years, so timing the exit matters more than timing the entry.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (23.24x, reached by the 18-month column).

To 31 December 2027+60.3%+49.1%41.57+7.8%+26.9%+20.1%
To 30 June 2029+79.6%+24.4%46.57+14.0%+53.4%+8.0%

What drives the model's return. The arithmetic is honest about its own shape:

  • The dividend leg (7.8 points to December 2027; 14 points to mid-2029) is the $1.19 paid in 2026, plus $1.70 in 2027 and $1.80 a year thereafter: about 6-7% a year on today's price. I hold that assumption with 60% confidence until the February decision.
  • The earnings leg is large to December 2027 (+20 points), because the forward earnings years move from FY2026 ($1.93 on the model's basis) into the FY2027-28 peak ($2.30 and $2.22). It shrinks to +8 points by mid-2029, because by then the forward years are the FY2029 dip ($1.91) and the FY2030 recovery ($2.05). The earnings contribution peaks and then gives back, which is the fade of #6 expressed through the forward years.
  • The multiple leg (27 points, then 53) is a re-rating from 12.8x to 23.24x that I do not expect, for the reasons in #11. It accounts for the whole difference between the model's return and mine.

The return at my fair multiple of 12-13x. The useful return is in the first six to nine months. By spring 2027, FY2027 consensus EPS should have risen 7-10% towards $2.25-2.35 and the dividend should be confirmed, while the forward years the market prices (FY2027-28) are still at their peak. After spring 2027 the forward years roll down, and the holder is paid the dividend to watch EPS fall.

Strongest counter-case. If the bulls are right that 2028 is a second peak year ($2.50-2.70 of EPS), the forward EPS in December 2027 is about $2.5 rather than $2.07, and 13x gives €29-30 plus dividends: a total return of about +20%. That is the real upside case, and it rests on the policy floor holding and on restocking not ending, both outside the company's control.

What would change my view. The same signals as in #10: the February outlook and dividend for the near-term leg; and distributor inventories, imports and the August 2027 outlook for whether the forward earnings years hold up.

Score: 23, set by the Rater. A small weighted loss gives an F, and a return of about -1% maps to about 24. I move it down one point for the fat lower tail (a fair trough 35-45% below the price on a tariff reversal). The near-term +5-10% over six to nine months and the three-year check of +3% to +9% keep it at the top of the band.

#13. Summary conclusion

Tenaris is a high-quality cyclical, with the best balance sheet, the widest service moat and the most reliable guidance culture in its industry. It is entering the four quarters in which a policy-and-restocking price rent reaches its income statement, a conservative guide steps up, a stale consensus is corrected by 7-10%, and a doubled dividend is confirmed at about a 6% yield. The investment case is therefore front-loaded: own the reinforcing leg into February and the spring, treat the second half of 2027 as the exit window, and do not pay for a re-rating that the evidence does not support.

Why own the shares now

Each of the four near-term positives is observable before it is reported, and the probability that the next two events deliver them is about 70-80%. The case is simple and trackable: two external variables, published monthly, set about 85% of the outcome.

Why exit in the second half of 2027

The same simplicity is the warning. The price rent ends when distributors are full and imports and three named US mills respond. The Gulf reopening that restores $85m a quarter of EBITDA also lowers the oil price that feeds operators' 2028 budgets. The operating leverage that turns 10% revenue growth into 20% EBITDA growth in 2027 works at a 70% decremental margin on the way down. And the multiple has already re-rated to the top decile of five years, in a history where the stock's high multiples belong to trough earnings, not to peaks like this one.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 55, set by the Rater. A strong, dated external force (topic 1 at 66) reaches profits with high certainty in FY2027, with EBITDA up 20% and EPS up 14%, but internal change is a mild net negative for EPS (48). The financial outputs do not improve enough over the thesis horizon (topic 6 at D: EPS flat from FY2025 to FY2029, and consensus EPS growth over two to three years at the 4th percentile). The net change is therefore a mild positive concentrated in one year, below the memo's B.

Foundations' Robustness: 72, set by the Rater. A premium oligopoly position with organisational switching costs, $3.56bn of net cash and a 20% margin floor (topic 3 at 70) is backed by a strong, repeatable beat record (topic 4 at 72). That would be the 75 band, but earnings swing widely with the cycle, the margin lead over Vallourec has closed and governance puts the controlling shareholder first, so Tenaris sits just below it, in line with the memo's B.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 50, set by the Rater. The best fit is a Demand-driven EPS Upgrader, but the step-up is mostly a policy-and-restocking price rent rather than a durable shift in demand. Only deepwater, a fifth of sales, is structural demand, and the earnings step reverses from 2028. The case therefore fits the setup in kind while missing its key element, durable demand. I score the fit in substance only and leave the top-of-range multiple to topics 11 and 12, which is why it sits at 50, in line with the memo's C.

Case Riskiness: 42, set by the Rater. The case is simple, rests on two monthly trackable drivers and carries no balance-sheet tail. But a sudden policy binary (Section 232), a cyclical peak that precedents put 6-12 months away, a down-skewed FY2027 EPS range of -24% to +10% and a fair trough 35-45% below the price make the outcome riskier than typical, consistent with topic 9 at 42 and the memo's C.

End notes

Sources: the memo text is the Investment Analyst's draft of 4 November 2026, edited for clarity by the Copy Editor. Default charts and tables come from Viewforth's dashboard files and FactSet, with their own notes beneath each. Charts marked "Drawn from" were drawn by the Visual Editor from figures stated in the memo, in the house style; the chart of the four judgements in #0 was drawn by the Copy Editor from the judgement table.

Conventions: money is in US dollars unless stated. The share price is in euros: €25.93, about $29.05 a share; one American depositary share (NYSE: TS) represents two ordinary shares. EBITDA is on the company's own basis. The model's EPS is stated before minority interests; wherever this memo compares EPS with reported or consensus figures, which are both after minorities, it quotes the model's EPS after minorities, about $0.06 a share lower. Consensus is shown by named financial year. Share counts use the 1,009.6m shares in issue.

Terms: OCTG is oil country tubular goods, the casing and tubing used in oil and gas wells. Rig Direct is Tenaris's service model, in which it runs pipe supply and logistics directly for the customer's rigs. Section 232 is the US national-security tariff on steel imports, now 50% on full customs value. San Faustin is Tenaris's controlling shareholder (the Rocca family's holding company, which also controls Ternium and Tecpetrol through the Techint group). PipeLogix publishes the US OCTG price index; PortWatch tracks Hormuz shipping transits. Two-year-forward P/E divides the share price by average EPS over the next two financial years.

Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. All scores are set by the Rater.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
